# Developing an AI-TPACK framework: exploring the mediating role of AI attitudes in pre-service TCSL teachers’ self-efficacy and AI-TPACK

**Guanyao Xu1** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3964-5941) **Aiqing Yu2** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0003-1869-8016) **Anna Gao3,4** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0009-0004-4702-5843) **Guy Trainin5**

Received: 16 December 2024 / Accepted: 20 May 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

**Abstract** Teachers’ technological knowledge is essential for integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language education. Additionally, teachers’ self-efficacy and attitudes to- ward AI can foster the integration of AI tools in education. This study developed an Artificial Intelligence – Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI- TPACK) framework to measure the specific knowledge and skills required for pre- service teachers specializing in teaching Chinese as a second language (TCSL) to effectively integrate AI into their teaching practices. A total of 520 pre-service TCSL teachers participated in the study. The development of the AI-TPACK frame- work involved Explanatory Factor Analysis (EFA) with 284 participants and Confir- matory Factor Analysis (CFA) with 236 participants to evaluate the model fit. The finalized framework consists of 25 items, encompassing seven dimensions: Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), AI-Technological Knowledge (AI- TK), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), AI-Technological Content Knowl- edge (AI-TCK), AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK), and the synthesized form AI-TPACK. Furthermore, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to examined how pre-service TCSL teachers’ self-efficacy influences their AI-TPACK, focusing on the mediating role of AI attitudes. The results demon- strated that pre-service TCSL teachers’ self-efficacy significantly influences their AI-TPACK through direct and indirect pathways, with AI attitudes serving as the mediating factor. This study made several recommendations for future professional development programs, emphasizing the need to bolster teachers’ self-efficacy and enhance their positive attitudes toward AI to better prepare them for the evolving language educational landscape.

**Keywords** Artificial intelligence – technological pedagogical content knowledge (AI-TPACK) · Teachers’ self-efficacy · AI attitudes · Pre-service teacher · Teaching Chinese as a second language (TCSL)

Extended author information available on the last page of the article

**1 Introduction**

Technology integration in education has influenced both learner’s study modes and teacher’s education and professional development (Chen et al., 2022). The Techno- logical Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and the assessment instrument have been developed to conceptualize the critical knowledge teach- ers need to integrate technology into teaching practice (Mishra & Koehler, 2006; Schmidt et al., 2009). The TPACK framework, consisting of content, pedagogy, and technology knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006), extends the Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) model (Shulman, 1986, 1987) by incorporating technology to meet the needs of the digital era. It is one of the frameworks that serves as a theo- retical basis for understanding teachers’ information and communication technology expertise and provides a scaffold for effective technology integration in education (Mishra & Koehler, 2006; Mishra et al., 2023).

Over time, educational technology has undergone a significant transformation in the realm of language education (Xu et al., 2024). Notably, Artificial Intelligence (AI) emerges as a groundbreaking advancement, introducing a new era within educational technology (Timotheou et al., 2023). With the increasing use of AI, effectively inte- grating AI into education requires teachers to possess specific technological and ped- agogical knowledge, which necessitates an expansion of the TPACK framework to align with the growing implementation of AI technology (Ning et al., 2024). Several theoretical models have been proposed to conceptualize the integration of AI educa- tion into the TPACK framework. For instance, Ng et al. (2021) revised the TPACK framework to evaluate teachers’ competencies and the impact of AI on their teaching and learning. Sun et al. (2023) developed a professional development program rooted in the TPACK framework to enhance the AI instructional capabilities of in-service teachers of computer science. Celik (2023) developed a scale to measure teachers’ knowledge for utilizing instructional AI based on TPACK frameworks, extending it with ethical aspects in the proposed framework.

Despite these advancements, most current AI-TPACK frameworks focus on gen- eral educators, leaving a significant gap in frameworks tailored for second language (L2) education teachers. L2 education, especially teaching Chinese as a second lan- guage (TCSL), presents unique challenges, such as adapting AI tools to the linguis- tic and cultural nuances of Chinese language instruction (Xu et al., 2024). Without a framework specifically designed for this context, pre-service TCSL teachers may struggle to develop the competencies needed to integrate AI effectively. As Ning et al. (2023) emphasized, the AI-TPACK framework requires further examination and validation in diverse educational contexts, including L2 education. Developing an AI-inclusive TPACK framework for pre-service TCSL teachers will help address this gap and provide a more accurate evaluation of their readiness to integrate AI into their teaching practices.

Teachers’ technology integration competency is influenced by various factors (McCulloch et al., 2018). Barriers that hinder teachers from integrating technology into education often arise from their beliefs regarding the effectiveness of technol- ogy (Ertmer et al., 2012). Consequently, the TPACK framework has not only been adapted and extended but also explored in relation to other concepts, such as teach-

ers’ self-efficacy (TSE; Abbitt, [2011)](#declarations)and attitudes (Dong et al., 2020; Scherer et al., 2018). Among these factors, teachers’ attitudes play a crucial role in the adoption of technology, including AI tools (Gil-Flores et al., 2017; Durak, 2021; Njiku, 2023). TPACK and teachers’ attitude have been studied together in various studies which demonstrated their significance on technology application (Njiku, 2023; Raygan & Moradkhani, 2022). However, while prior studies have explored general attitudes (Malinen et al., 2012; Weber & Greiner, 2019), little attention has been given to attitudes specifically toward AI. Furthermore, limited research has investigated how TSE and AI attitudes (AI-AT) interact to influence AI-TPACK, particularly in the context of pre-service TCSL teachers.

This study aims to develop and validate an AI-TPACK framework within the con- text of L2 education, with a specific focus on pre-service TCSL teachers. Additionally, this research seeks to investigate the impact of TSE on teachers’ AI-TPACK, particu- larly by confirming the mediator role of attitudes towards AI technology. By assess- ing teachers’ AI-TPACK knowledge and attitudes towards AI, valuable insights can be gained to better prepare teachers for integrating AI technology into the classroom. Through an exploration of the relationship between TSE, attitudes towards AI, and AI-TPACK, a comprehensive understanding can be achieved across these research domains. The results indicate that the self-efficacy of pre-service TCSL teachers sig- nificantly influences their AI-TPACK, with AI attitudes acting as a mediator.

**2 Theoretical framework**

**2.1 Evolving TPACK with AI**

TPACK is a framework that integrates technology into the teaching process, based on the PCK model (Shulman, 1986, 1987). The TPACK framework has evolved over time with the continuous advancement of technology. It has been extended by incorporating self-efficacy beliefs toward technology, transforming into the TPACK Self-Efficacy Scale (TPACK-SeS) framework, using subsequent quantitative meth- ods (Bilici et al., 2013). Furthermore, it has been associated with teacher’s pedagogi- cal use of the Web and has explored the relationship between teacher’s self-efficacy and the TPCK-W, which informs insights on improving teacher professional devel- opment (Lee & Tsai, 2010). The development and validation of the 21 st century TPACK (TPACK-21) model have integrated the TPACK framework with skills rel- evant to the twenty-first century, such as collaboration and critical thinking (Valtonen et al., 2017). Recognized for its flexibility and dynamism, TPACK has been studied from various perspectives (Schmid et al., 2024; Valtonen et al., 2017). This frame- work not only provides valuable insights into teacher education but also serves as a benchmark for assessing both pre-service and in-service teachers’ proficiency in integrating technology effectively using a variety of assessment tools and methods (Schmid et al., 2024).

In recent times, researchers have introduced the AI-TPACK framework, an exten- sion of the TPACK model, to support educators in effectively integrating AI-based applications into teaching practices and enhancing their understanding of AI tool 

integration in education (Celik, 2023; Lodge et al., 2023; Mishra et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2024). It was highlighted that AI has similar qualities like other digital tech- nologies with a revolutionary breakthrough affecting specific knowledge domains of TPACK (Mishra et al., 2023). Yue et al. (2024) proposed an AI-TPACK framework with seven elements– Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), Tech- nological Knowledge (TK), Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Content Knowledge (TCK), Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK), and one synthesized form (TPACK) – mirroring the seven knowledge forms of the TPACK model. Celik (2023) further contributed to the development of the AI-TPACK frame- work by refining it and delineating five fundamental components, namely AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, AI-TPACK, and Ethics. However, existing AI-enhanced frame- works primarily assess the level of knowledge and skills for general educators. There is a noticeable gap in research concerning the assessment of AI-TPACK specifically tailored for teachers in L2 education. Developing an AI-inclusive TPACK framework specifically designed for pre-service TCSL teachers will help address the research gap and enhance the evaluation of educators’ readiness to effectively integrate AI technologies.

**2.2 The role of teachers’ self-efficacy in AI-TPACK**

TPACK has been extensively studied alongside psychological concepts such as teacher self-efficacy and attitudes (Durak, 2019). Self-efficacy refers to one’s per- ceived abilities within a specific domain. In the context of teaching, TSE is con- ceptualized as their perceptions of their ability in facilitating students’ knowledge within a discipline (Lee & Tsai, 2010). According to self-efficacy theory, beliefs regarding one’s ability to influence expected outcomes shape actions and thoughts. Consequently, self-efficacy is recognized as a significant factor influencing teachers’ integration of technology (Abbitt, [2011;](#declarations) Durak, 2019; Ertmer et al., 2012). Previous research has shown that TSE significantly impacts their TPACK levels and influences their actions related to technology integration in the classroom, acting as a positive predictor of their actions and intentions (Dong et al., 2020; Holden & Rada, 2011). Building upon these findings, this study aims to explore the potential mediating factors between TSE and their AI-TPACK.

**2.3 The potential mediating role of teachers’ AI attitudes**

Previous studies have emphasized the significance of teachers’ attitudes toward tech- nology, highlighting attitudes’ pivotal role in the effective integration of technology (Farjon et al., 2019; Gil-Flores et al., 2017; Durak, 2021; Njiku, 2023). A large body of literature underscores that attitudes toward technology are crucial determinants of successful technology integration (Durak, 2019; Scherer et al., 2018), demonstrat- ing a strong positive correlation with TPACK (Njiku, 2023; Scherer et al., 2018). Furthermore, prior research has explored the connection between attitudes and self- efficacy (Malinen et al., 2012; Weber & Greiner, 2019), yet limited attention has been given to the interaction between attitudes toward AI and TSE.

In this research, teachers’ AI attitudes (AI-AT) are defined as teachers’ specific feelings that reflect their likes or dislikes to the use of AI technology. This study seeks to investigate the mediating role of AI-AT in the relationship between TSE and AI-TPACK in addition to expanding the TPACK framework by incorporating AI technology. Figure 1 illustrates the research model of this study. The hypothesis posits that TSE can influence pre-service TCSL teachers’ AI-TPACK through their attitudes toward AI.

**2.4 Questions guiding this study**

Based on the research model proposed, this study aims to investigate the following research questions:

1. Is the proposed AI-TPACK framework valid and reliable for pre-service TCSL teachers?
2. Can TSE directly influence pre-service TCSL teachers’ AI-TPACK?
3. Can TSE indirectly influence pre-service TCSL teachers’ AI-TPACK through the mediating effects of attitudes toward AI?

**3 Methodology**

**3.1 Participants**

The participants were from eight different universities across China, each with national rankings ranging from the top 20 to 250. All participants were majoring in International Chinese Education. The survey was conducted using Wenjuanxing, 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1** The research model a research-qualified web-based survey tool (Xu et al., 2024). Initially, 596 pre-ser- vice TCSL teachers were invited to take part. Ultimately, 542 questionnaires were received, of which 520 contained valid responses, reflecting an 87.2% valid response rate.

The descriptive statistics are presented in Table 1. Out of 520 respondents, 461 (88.7%) were female and 59 (11.3%) were male. This gender imbalance reflected the actual gender ratio in the pre-service TCSL teacher community. Two hundred and seventy-nine (53.7%) had teaching experience, whereas 241 (46.3%) did not. Partici- pants with teaching experience slightly outnumbered those without. Regarding the grade level, 242 (46.5%) were undergraduate students, while 278 (53.5%) were mas- ter’s students. The undergraduate sample exclusively comprised Juniors and Seniors who had completed the most major and elective courses within the teacher education program. Previous literature has often used Juniors and Seniors as the sample for studying pre-service teachers (e.g., Baser et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2024). Furthermore, the Center for Language Education and Cooperation (CLEC), an institution affiliated with the Chinese Ministry of Education, frequently selects students from this group to serve as volunteer TCSL teachers abroad.

To develop and validate the AI-TPACK framework, the full dataset of 520 partici- pants was randomly split into two subsets: 284 participants for Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and 236 participants for Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). These subsets were used to assess the validity and reliability of the proposed framework. For the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) analysis addressing research questions 2 and 3 (the relationships between TSE, AI-AT, and AI-TPACK), the full dataset of 520 participants was utilized. Participants were guaranteed the confidentiality and anonymity of their responses, and informed consent was obtained before their participation.

**3.2 Instruments**

In this study, three scales were utilized: teachers’ AI-TPACK, TSE, and AI-AT.

**3.2.1 Scales of AI-TPACK**

To assess teachers’ AI-specific technological and pedagogical knowledge, we reviewed existing studies on TPACK scales and the pedagogical foundations of AI tools to develop our framework. The proposed AI-TPACK framework was formu- lated based on Celik’s (2023) five-dimensional framework and Ning et al.’s (2024) seven-dimensional framework. Celik’s framework includes AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI- TPK, AI-TPACK, and Ethics, while Ning et al.’s framework consists of PK, CK, AI-TK, PCK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, and AI-TPACK itself. These two frameworks were designed for teachers applying AI technology in general education rather than for specific teaching contexts.

Through modifying the items from Celik and Ning et al.’s frameworks, 29 items were initially generated across seven dimensions, tailored specifically for TCSL teaching. Figure 2 illustrates the preliminary scale of the proposed AI-TPACK framework.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2** The preliminary scale of AI-TPACK

**3.2.2 Scales of teachers’ self-efficacy (TSE) and AI attitude (AI-AT)**

The TSE scale developed by Schwarzer has been widely used and translated into more than 25 languages (Schwarzer et al., 1999). The Chinese version of this scale was also validated (Zhang & Schwarzer, 1995). In this study, a TSE scale, based on the works of Schwarzer and Jerusalem (1995) and Smith and Hung (2017), was developed to assess participants’ TSE using a total of six items (refer to Appendix [1)](#appendix1-items-for-teachers-self-efficacy-tse-scale). Minor modifications were made to ensure relevance to the current study’s focus. The internal consistency of the developed scale was evaluated using Cronbach’s alpha. In our study, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the scale was 0.895, indicating good reliability (Fornell & Larcker, 1981).

Grassini (2023) developed a 4-item AI-AT scale to evaluate public perceptions of AI technology. The four items of the scale aimed to assess: (1) personal beliefs about benefits of AI, (2) perceived usefulness of AI, (3) individual’s intentions for AI adop- tion, and (4) concerns about the risks of AI. The first three items of Grassini’s scale were derived from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which emphasizes the significance of perceived usefulness in technology acceptance (Davis, 1989). Our study utilized a modified AI-AT framework with three items, omitting the aspect related to “3) individual’s intentions for AI adoption” from Grassini’s (2023) scale, considering teachers’ presumed readiness to integrate AI into their teaching practices (refer to Appendix [2)](#appendix1-items-for-teachers-self-efficacy-tse-scale). Furthermore, minor adjustments were also made to align the scale with the specific focus of this study on TCSL education. Notably, the proposed scale demonstrated good internal consistency with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.881, indicating high reliability (Fornell & Larcker, 1981).

**3.2.3 The use of surveys**

In this study, the questionnaire encompassing the three scales (AI-TPACK, TSE, and AI-AT) was provided in both English and Chinese languages. All items were trans- lated into Chinese using back-translation procedures to ensure the appropriateness of the survey questions (Wind et al., 2021). Participants rated the questionnaires on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (indicating “strongly disagree”) to 5 (indicating “strongly agree”).

**3.3 Data analysis**

The data analysis process consisted of three stages: EFA, CFA, and SEM. To address research question 1, the developed AI-TPACK scale was validated by conducting the EFA and CFA. The factorability of the scale was assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer- Olkin (KMO) measure and the Bartlett’s test of sphericity. Model fit was evaluated using various indices (Hu & Bentler, 1999): Normed Chi-square ( χ 2_/_df) with val- ues of 2.00 or lower suggested a good fit, Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) where a value equal to or greater than 0.90 indicated acceptable fit, Comparative Fit Index (CFI) with a threshold of 0.90 was deemed for acceptable fit, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) where values of 0.08 or lower were considered acceptable, and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) with values of 0.08 or lower indicated a good fit. Additionally, Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficients and factor loadings were computed. The average variance extracted (AVE) and composite reli- ability (CR) were calculated to evaluate the convergent validity of the scale. To address research questions 2 and 3, SEM was employed to examine the asso- ciation between TSE and AI-TPACK, with AI-AT serving as the mediator. The path analysis was performed using the aforementioned criteria: χ 2_/_df, TLI, CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR (Hu & Bentler, 1999). Cronbach’s alpha, AVE, and CR were calculated to assess the reliability of the model, and the significance of paths among TSE, AI-AT, and AI-TPACK was analyzed. Following this, a bootstrapping analysis was employed to determine the significance of the indirect effect, utilizing a bias- corrected bootstrapping procedure with 5000 bootstrap samples.

In the process of conducting SEM, the data selected for AI-TPACK was derived from the synthesized dimension within the developed AI-TPACK framework, which unifies CK, PK, and AI-TK. Prior studies, such as Bai et al. ([2024)](#declarations), have also employed this synthesized form. This approach to data selection enables a more comprehensive evaluation of teachers’ competencies in utilizing AI within the realms of pedagogy and content knowledge. Through the utilization of this integrated ver- sion of AI-TPACK, a more comprehensive assessment of teachers’ competencies in leveraging AI is achieved.

**4.1 AI-TPACK scale development**

Prior to conducting EFA, the data was checked to determine its suitability for reveal- ing factors. The KMO value was calculated as 0.932, exceeding the recommended

results affirm the validity of proceeding with the EFA, as the data exhibits strong suitability for factor extraction.

After the initial round of EFA, four items (CK4, PK1, PCK4, AI-TPK4) from the proposed AI-TPACK framework were removed due to low factor loadings (\< 0.5) and significant cross-loadings (Hair et al., 2018). Subsequently, 25 items were retained, resulting in a total scale Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.944. The fit indices of EFA ( χ 2_/_df = 1.693, TLI = 0.933, CFI = 0.963, RMSEA = 0.066, SRMR = 0.024) dem- onstrated that the measurement model had good validity (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The framework maintained the same seven dimensions as the proposed preliminary scale: CK, PK, AI-TK, PCK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, and AI-TPACK. Following this analysis, all remaining items demonstrated factor loadings above 0.5, with specifics on the fac- tor loadings of each item provided in Table 2.

To examine the structural validity of the seven-dimensional AI-TPACK frame- work within language education, a CFA was conducted. The CFA results revealed favorable fit indices with a χ 2_/_df of 1.727, TLI of 0.930, CFI of 0.940, RMSEA of 0.068, and SRMR of 0.058, indicating a well-fitting model (Hu & Bentler, 1999).

Table 3 illustrated the construct validity of the developed framework. The fac- tor loadings of the 25 items ranged from 0.651 to 0.929, demonstrating the items’ strong associations with their factor (Hair et al., 2018). All seven factors exhibited factor loadings exceeding the 0.5 threshold, ranging from 0.541 to 0.809, signifying significant relationships with the proposed framework (Hair et al., 2018). The AVE values for the seven factors ranged from 0.628 to 0.780. These values indicated that between 62.8% and 78.0% of the variance in the observed variables is accounted for by the latent constructs, suggesting satisfactory convergent validity (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). The CR values for the factors varied from 0.845 to 0.934. These val- ues exceeded the threshold of 0.7, with some dimensions even surpassing 0.9, indi- cating high internal consistency and reliability of the measurement model (George & Mallery, 2019). Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficients of each factor were between 0.806 and 0.893, and the overall coefficient for the 25-item framework was 0.944. These results collectively reinforce the robustness and reliability of the developed AI-TPACK framework for enhancing teaching practices in the context of TCSL edu- cation. The mean scores for these factors ranged from 3.602 to 4.186 on a 5-point Likert scale, indicat- ing high levels of responses (Oxford & Burry-Stock, 1995). Among these factors, CK received the highest score (Mean = 4.186, SD = 0.706), which suggests a high level of confidence in delivering TCSL instruction. Conversely, AI-TPK received the lowest score (Mean = 3.602, SD = 0.702), which implies the potential gaps in understanding how the use of AI transforms the teaching and learning processes in TCSL education. **4.3 Mediation analysis**

In the initial phase of the analysis, Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated among the variables TSE, AI-AT, and AI-TPACK. The descriptive statistics of the variables and their bivariate correlations are shown in Table 6. The results indicated a significant positive correlation between TSE and AI-AT (_r_ = 0.555, _p_ \< 0.01) and a moderate positive correlation between AI-AT and AI-TPACK (_r_ = 0.447, _p_ \< 0.01). Additionally, a significant positive correlation was observed between TSE and AI- TPACK (_r_ = 0.488, _p_ \< 0.01).

Subsequently, a SEM was constructed to further investigate research questions 2 and 3. The path analysis tested a mediation model that examines both the direct impact of TSE on AI-TPACK and the indirect influence of TSE on AI-TPACK medi- ated by the variable AI-AT. The model exhibited acceptable fitting indices: χ 2_/_df = 2.561, CFI = 0.960, TLI = 0.951, RMSEA = 0.070, and SRMR = 0.037. Evaluating

The analysis presented in Table 7 assesses the reliability and validity of the model. The Cronbach’s alpha values for each scale (AI-TPACK, TSE, AI-AT) are all above 0.7, indicating satisfactory internal consistency across the instruments. The CR val- ues for the three scales ranged from 0.878 to 0.895, demonstrating robust internal consistency within each scale. The AVE values for these scales ranged from 0.544 to 0.780, surpassing the recommended threshold of 0.5 (Fornell & Larcker, 1981) and illustrating strong convergent validity within each construct. The results delineated the mediation model and estimated both direct and indirect effects within the model. Figure 3 presents the path diagram of the model. The results indicated that AI- TPACK received direct paths from TSE (β = 0.322, SE = 0.084, _p_ \< 0.001) and AI-AT (β = 0.288, SE = 0.078, _p_ \< 0.001). Additionally, TSE had a substantial positive effect on AI-AT (β = 0.570, SE = 0.056, _p_ \< 0.001). Partial mediation implies that there is a

These pathways suggest that TSE influences AI- TPACK both directly and indirectly through AI-AT, which serves as a partial mediator. The bootstrapping analysis was next employed to evaluate the significance of the indirect effect. Table 8 presents the analysis results. The direct effect of TSE on AI- TPACK was statistically significant, explaining 68.4% of the total effect. The indi- rect path contributed 31.6% to the total effect. This pattern is consistent with partial mediation, where the mediator explains a portion of the relationship, while the direct effect remains significant.

**5 Discussion**

**5.1 The proposed AI-TPACK framework**

The first research question in this study aimed to develop and validate an AI-TPACK framework for evaluating pre-service TCSL teachers’ knowledge and skills in inte- grating AI into teaching practices. Through EFA, seven potential dimensions were identified, followed by CFA to confirm the seven-factor structure’s validity. The results established the proposed AI-TPACK framework as a reliable and valid assess- ment tool. Hence, it is confidently asserted that the proposed framework is valid and reliable for pre-service TCSL teachers.

The developed AI-TPACK framework provides a practical tool for assessing L2 educators’ readiness to integrate AI technology into their teaching practices. Teacher education programs are recommended to adopt this framework to design targeted workshops and training sessions that help pre-service teachers build the knowledge and skills necessary for effective AI integration. For example, workshops could teach pre-service teachers to use AI-powered language learning applications, such as auto- mated writing evaluators, to enhance students’ learning outcomes. Training sessions might include hands-on activities where pre-service teachers design lesson plans that integrate AI tools to address specific L2 learning challenges, such as fostering inter- active speaking exercises. Additionally, in-service L2 teachers can use the framework as a self-assessment tool to identify areas for professional growth and enhance their competencies in AI-supported pedagogy. By addressing these gaps, teachers can pur-

sue targeted professional development opportunities, ensuring they remain proficient in integrating AI technologies into their teaching practices.

The AI-TPACK evaluation among pre-service TCSL teachers offered valuable insights into their perceptions and competencies. Notably, respondents rated CK high- est that indicates their confidence in delivering subject-specific instruction, aligned with the traditional emphasis on subject matter content knowledge (Shulman, 1986). The high score in CK also suggests that pre-service TCSL teachers were well-trained in substantial academic content. However, AI-TPK received the lowest score, sug- gesting challenges in effectively integrating AI tools into pedagogical practices. This difficulty may stem from a lack of specialized training in AI-enhanced pedagogy. Moving beyond theoretical understanding, hands-on experiences can empower pre- service teachers to engage actively with AI technologies and foster practical skills through direct experience and reflection (Koehler et al., 2013). Thus, integrating practical experiences into teachers’ education programs may bridge the gap in AI- TPK proficiency and enhance pedagogical strategies. Teachers’ education programs are recommended to include hands-on workshops, simulated teaching environments, and real classroom placements to allow pre-service teachers to actively engage with AI technologies in pedagogical settings.

The AI-TCK, PK, and AI-TK domains received similar scores, with ratings rang- ing from No. 2 to No. 4. The paired sample t-test indicated no significant differences among AI-TCK, PK, and AI-TK, implying that pre-service TCSL teachers did not distinctly rate their competencies or understanding in these fields. The results suggest that pre-service TCSL teachers grasp how AI tools can aid Chinese language learn- ing; exhibit confidence in general teaching strategies, which is also a focal point in most teachers’ training programs (Darling-Hammond, 2017); and possess the knowl- edge to effectively utilize AI technology. These findings indicate a readiness among pre-service TCSL teachers to engage in continuous professional development in AI educational technology. Therefore, teachers’ education programs are recommended to focus on integrating AI tools more extensively into the curriculum to further enhance pre-service teachers’ technological competencies related to AI and support their continuous professional development in educational technology.

**5.2 Influence of TSE on AI-TPACK in TCSL education**

The second research question aimed to examine whether TSE can directly influence pre-service TCSL teachers’ AI-TPACK. In this study, TSE was defined as pre-ser- vice TCSL teachers’ perceptions of their ability to enhance students’ understand- ing and knowledge. The observed significant positive correlation between TSE and AI-TPACK indicated that higher levels of self-efficacy are associated with a greater proficiency in integrating AI technologies into TCSL education practices. The path analysis and bootstrapping procedures conducted within SEM further confirmed this relationship, revealing a direct pathway from TSE to AI-TPACK. These findings align with prior research emphasizing the crucial role of self-efficacy in technology integration (Abbitt, [2011;](#declarations) Durak, 2019; Ertmer et al., 2012).

The findings suggest that fostering TSE has direct practical implications for teacher training and professional development. Higher TSE can play a key role in 

accelerating the adoption of AI-based teaching practices. This is especially relevant in language education, where AI tools are increasingly used to enhance L2 learning by providing automated feedback, enabling personalized learning, and offering intel- ligent tutoring (Xu et al., 2025). Teachers with higher self-efficacy are more likely to embrace these tools effectively. For instance, pre-service TCSL teachers with stron- ger self-efficacy may feel more confident in creating AI-enhanced teaching materials or using AI tools like chatbots to support language learning. These findings under- score the crucial role of TSE in shaping teachers’ competency in effectively utilizing AI tools to enhance teaching practices. Furthermore, this conclusion was consistent with previous research that shows TSE is a positive predictor of teachers’ actions related to technology integration, significantly influencing the development of their technological knowledge and skills (Dong et al., 2020; Durak, 2019; López-Vargas et al., 2017; Semiz & Ince, 2012; Wang et al., 2024).

TSE directly influences AI-TPACK, and according to social cognitive theory which posits that individuals learn through observation, imitation, and reinforce- ment (Bandura, [1988)](#declarations), the development in AI-TPACK can also enhance TSE. As individuals observe successful implementation of AI technologies and receive posi- tive feedback on their own mastery of AI-TPACK, they are more likely to perceive themselves as competent educators. This process of observational learning and posi- tive reinforcement can lead to increased confidence in improving students’ learning, consequently contributing to higher levels of TSE. This creates a positive feedback loop where teachers’ perceptions of their ability to proficiently use AI technology enhances their AI-TPACK capabilities. As AI-TPACK skills improve, they in turn boost confidence levels, thus establishing a continuous cycle of mutual reinforce- ment. Consequently, this iterative process leads to a sustained enhancement of teach- ers’ confidence and competence in applying AI technologies effectively in TCSL educational settings, enabling them to transform their theoretical knowledge into practical teaching strategies.

To build TSE effectively, teacher education programs can adopt several practical strategies that provide pre-service teachers with mastery experiences, which Bandura (1997) and Orakcı et al. (2023) identify as critical for developing TSE. First, hands- on workshops and scenario-based training allow pre-service teachers to practice using AI tools in low-stakes environments, directly enhancing their self-efficacy by providing opportunities to experience success in integrating AI technology. Second, mentorship initiatives pairing pre-service teachers with experienced educators can provide guidance and modeling, helping to strengthen pre-service teachers’ belief in their ability to implement AI effectively. Third, participation in AI-focused work- shops, seminars, and conferences can expose pre-service teachers to the latest techno- logical advancements, reinforcing their confidence in staying competent and relevant in their teaching practices. Beyond pre-service education, these strategies can also be adapted for in-service teachers, ensuring they continue to develop self-efficacy and proficiency in leveraging AI to improve teaching outcomes. By bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application, these initiatives empower teachers to integrate AI tools with confidence and competence in their classrooms.

**5.3 The mediating effects of attitudes toward AI**

The third research question in this study aimed to investigate the mediating role of AI-AT between pre-service TCSL teachers’ TSE and AI-TPACK. In this research, AI-AT was defined as teachers’ specific feelings that indicate their preferences towards the utilization of AI technology. The results of the study underscore the significant influence of AI-AT. The mediating role of AI-AT was observed to play a moderate but important role, consistent with a partial mediation model. TSE influences AI-TPACK through both direct and indirect pathways. While the direct effect of TSE on AI- TPACK was stronger, the indirect effect via AI-AT was statistically significant, high- lighting the importance of teachers’ attitudes toward AI in enhancing their ability to integrate AI into teaching. These findings suggest the importance of considering both self-efficacy beliefs and attitudes towards AI technology in enhancing pre-service teachers’ abilities to integrate AI effectively into their teaching practices. The findings of the study are consistent with previous research that highlights the direct influence of TSE on attitudes towards AI, as observed in Durak (2019). Moreover, the positive correlation between higher attitudes towards technology and a more advanced TPACK level, as evidenced by studies conducted by Hew and Brush (2007), Scherer et al. (2018), and Njiku (2023), further supports the results of this study. These results reinforce the practical need for teacher education programs to focus on developing both technological competence and positive attitudes toward AI, ensuring pre-service teachers are both skilled and motivated to adopt AI tools. This study contributes by highlighting the importance of teachers’ perceptions of their ability to enhance students’ learning. It suggests that these perceptions not only serve as a motivational factor but also result in more positive attitudes toward the AI integration in L2 education.

Teacher education programs can greatly benefit from fostering positive AI-AT by placing emphasis on enhancing the self-efficacy of pre-service TCSL teachers. For instance, programs could integrate activities that demonstrate how AI tools enhance teaching outcomes, such as showcasing real-world applications of AI-powered L2 learning systems, to inspire pre-service teachers’ confidence and curiosity. By focus- ing on strengthening teachers’ perceived abilities, these programs can help cultivate more favorable AI-AT, which in turn increases teachers’ confidence and willingness to use AI tools in their teaching practices. Furthermore, by combining hands-on training workshops, mentorship initiatives, and immersive experiences designed to enhance TSE levels, teacher education programs can ensure that pre-service teachers not only develop positive AI-AT but also gain the confidence and skills needed to integrate AI tools effectively. This highlights how AI-AT serves as a pivotal mediator between TSE and AI-TPACK, complementing the direct influence of TSE on suc- cessful AI integration.

**5.4 Ethical implications of AI in education**

The integration of AI in L2 education brings transformative opportunities but also raises important ethical considerations. As highlighted by Chiu et al. (2024), teachers must navigate this complex landscape of AI integration with a strong ethical founda-

tion to ensure that AI tools are used responsibly and equitably in instruction. For pre- service TCSL teachers, this involves addressing issues such as data privacy, avoiding over-reliance on AI, and empowering students to engage with AI responsibly. Data privacy is at the forefront of ethical concerns in AI-assisted education. AI tools often require access to sensitive information, such students’ academic history, learning behaviors, and biometric data (Baker & Hawn, [2022)](#declarations). Without proper data protection frameworks, this data may be vulnerable to misuse, posing risks to both students and educators (Holmes et al., 2019). Pre-service TCSL teachers should be trained to implement best practices for protecting sensitive information, such as using secure AI platforms and adhering to data protection regulations. This aligns with Chiu et al.’s (2024) emphasis on safeguarding sensitive content to prevent breaches. Over-reliance on AI in teaching poses significant challenges for pre-service TCSL teachers, mirroring issues observed among students. As Zhai et al. (2024) noted, students’ excessive dependence on AI systems can weaken their critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical reasoning skills. Similarly, for pre-service teachers, over-reliance on AI tools, such as automated lesson planners, may reduce pedagogi- cal creativity and autonomy. Additionally, algorithmic biases (Baker & Hawn, [2022)](#declarations) and inaccuracies in AI tools (Williamson & Eynon, 2020) further highlight the risks of over-reliance. To address these challenges, teacher education programs should emphasize training pre-service TCSL teachers in AI literacy, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and the development of pedagogical skills that complement AI tools while reducing dependence on them.

Pre-service teachers play a key role in empowering students to engage responsibly with AI. As emphasized by Chiu et al. (2024), teachers should educate students about the ethical implications of AI, encouraging them to develop integrity and accountabil- ity in their interactions with technology. For example, TCSL educators can inspire students to critically evaluate AI-generated content, such as translations or grammar corrections, while underscoring the importance of cultural and contextual sensitivity. These efforts not only equip students to become knowledgeable AI users but also foster a learning environment that values ethical considerations and critical thinking.

**6 Conclusions**

This study expanded the application of AI-TPACK into the context of TCSL educa- tion through the development and validation of a new AI-TPACK framework. Addi- tionally, this research delved into how the self-efficacy of TCSL teachers influences their AI-TPACK, with a specific focus on the mediating role played by their attitudes toward AI. The key findings can be summarized as follows: Firstly, the results of EFA and CFA indicated that the proposed AI-TPACK framework, comprising seven fac- tors and 25 items, exhibits a strong model fit and serves as a reliable assessment tool. This framework can be used to measure TCSL teachers’ knowledge necessary for the effective integration of AI technology into teaching practices in both future research and practical applications. Secondly, within the domain of L2 education, this study revealed that TSE, defined as the perceived abilities of pre-service TCSL teachers in effectively improving students’ learning, directly contributes to the enhancement of teachers’ AI-TPACK. Lastly, the research highlighted the indirect influence of TSE on the AI-TPACK levels of pre-service TCSL teachers, mediated through their atti- tudes towards AI. These findings not only advance the theoretical comprehension of AI technology integration in L2 education but also provide practical insights for teachers seeking to enhance their AI-TPACK proficiency.

However, this research has identifiable limitations, which we summarize as fol- lows. First, the study focused on a specific group of pre-service TCSL teachers, which could limit the broader applicability of the results. Future research with more diverse samples could provide a more comprehensive understanding of teachers’ AI-TPACK. For instance, including in-service teachers or those teaching a different language could offer a more nuanced understanding of the implications drawn in this research. Second, in exploring the relationship between TSE, AI-AT, and AI-TPACK, this paper solely relies on surveys. Future research could consider employing mixed methods that allow for a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship, as qualitative data can provide contextual insights while quantitative data offers statisti- cal validation. Third, this study focused exclusively on AI-AT as the sole mediating factor in the relationship between TSE and AI-TPACK. However, other variables may also mediate or moderate this relationship. For example, factors such as prior experi- ence with AI, institutional support, or the perceived usefulness of AI tools may play significant roles in shaping teachers’ AI-TPACK. These factors may interact through more complex multi-level mediation or moderation pathways. Future research should examine these variables to gain deeper insights into the factors that influence educa- tors’ AI-TPACK development.

## Appendix 1: Items for teachers’ self-efficacy (TSE) scale

1. I can conduct lessons well.
2. I can clearly explain language and grammar points to learners.
3. I can achieve my teaching goals for every lesson.
4. I can have good class management.
5. I have my personal teaching style.
6. I can stay focused on and achieve my teaching goals with the aid of educational technology such as AI.

**Appendix 2 : Items for AI attitudes (AI-AT) scale**

1. I think AI can effectively assist language education.
2. I think educational technology can enhance learners’ language learning. I’ll apply educational technology such as AI in the future.
3. I think human beings can solve the risks posed by AI technology. It’s beneficial for assisting teachers and students.

## Appendix 3: Items for AI-TPACK framework

1\. **Content Knowledge (CK)** 

1.1 I completely understand the historical evolution of concepts and prin- ciples within my discipline.

1.2 I have a deep understanding of the knowledge structure of the content I teach.

1.3 I possess a substantial depth of subject-specific knowledge and am highly familiar with the instructional materials and curriculum standards.

2\. **Pedagogical Knowledge (PK)** 

2.1 I possess knowledge of effective classroom organization and management.

2.2 I take into consideration students’ backgrounds, interests, motivations, and other needs during teaching.

2.3 I am capable of using a variety of diverse teaching methods in the classroom.

3\. **AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK)** 

3.1 I am familiar with commonly encountered technologies including AI in the educational environment.

3.2 I possess the capability to easily acquire AI technologies necessary for teaching.

3.3 I frequently incorporate educational technologies including AI in the ped- agogical context.

3.4 I have the knowledge to resolve issues related to technologies including AI when encountered.

3.5 I am knowledgeable about using technology including AI for interactive teaching purposes.

4\. **Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK)** 

4.1 I am proficient at formulating curriculum plans with ease.

4.2 I prioritize analyzing students’ learning situations and am capable of alter- ing instructions to suit their individual needs.

4.3 I am well-acquainted with the focal points and challenging aspects of teaching.

5\. **AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK)** 

5.1 I am proficient in using educational technology, including AI tools based on the subject I am teaching.

5.2 I am proficient in using AI tools to update my knowledge base within the academic discipline.

5.3 I can select appropriate AI tools based on the subject I am teaching.

5.4 I am adept at using AI to effectively enhance students’ comprehension of the material.

6\. **AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK)** 

6.1 I am capable of using educational technologies including AI to enhance my pedagogical perspectives.

6.2 I am able to apply appropriate AI in various teaching activities.

6.3 I have the capacity to select AI to sustain students’ motivation and interest.

7. **Artificial Intelligence – Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK)** 

7.1 I am knowledgeable in integrating educational technology including AI with educational content and teaching methods to improve classroom teach- ing efficiency and effectiveness.

7.2 I am capable of selecting appropriate teaching methods and educational technology including AI based on the educational content for instruction.

7.3 I can use AI to create, simulate, and adapt scenarios that are in line with the educational content.

7.4 I can use personalized educational technology, including AI to select suit- able teaching methods as well as guide students in practical learning.
